opus-5.5.text:
I'm actually not that concerned, and I think it's worth explaining why, because the worry is natural if you take formal grammars literally. In a context-free grammar, you can in principle nest structures arbitrarily deep, and a network with a fixed number of layers clearly can't track unbounded recursion in a single forward pass. So from a strict computational standpoint, yes, there's a ceiling.

But two things soften that. First, real language doesn't use deep nesting very much. Humans themselves struggle beyond two or three levels of center embedding; sentences like "the rat the cat the dog chased ate died" are technically grammatical and practically incomprehensible. So the depth the data demands is modest, and a transformer with dozens of layers has plenty of room for what actually shows up.

Second, and this is closer to what we've studied with random hierarchical models, the interesting question isn't whether depth can represent the hierarchy, but how the hierarchy is learned from data. What we find is that the network builds up latent representations level by level, using correlations between tokens to group them into higher-level features, and each additional level of the hierarchy requires more data to be resolved, because the correlations that reveal it are weaker and span longer distances. So the bottleneck in practice is often sample complexity, not architectural depth. The model learns the shallow levels first and the deeper structure only as the training set grows.

There's also a looser point: depth in the network doesn't have to map one-to-one onto depth in the parse tree. Attention can combine information across positions in a single layer, and with chain-of-thought or autoregressive generation the model effectively gets extra computation steps. So the finite-depth limit is real in principle, but I'd say it's rarely the binding constraint. What matters more is understanding how much data you need to discover each layer of structure, and that's where I think the theory has the most to say.

r001.rationale: The candidate says finite depth is a real limit in principle but is rarely the binding constraint in practice.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'm not very concerned about it, and I think the reason is instructive.

If you take the formal view, yes, a transformer of depth L can only do a bounded number of sequential composition steps per token, so there are hierarchical structures, deeply nested center embeddings, long chains of brackets, that in principle it cannot resolve exactly. That's a real limitation and the theory papers are right to point it out.

But look at what the data actually require. Natural language is not a worst-case context-free language. Humans themselves fail at three or four levels of center embedding. The nesting depth that appears in real text is small and its distribution decays very fast. So the question is not "can the architecture handle arbitrary depth," it's "how much depth do you need to capture the statistics you are actually trained on," and the answer is: not much.

What we've been trying to understand in my group is something slightly different, which is how these models learn hierarchical structure at all, and how much data that takes. We've worked with synthetic generative models, random hierarchy models, where you can control the depth and the branching, and you see that the sample complexity grows with depth, but polynomially, not exponentially, because the network discovers the structure one level at a time. Lower-level features are learned first, then they get composed. And the depth of the network needed is set by the depth of the data's latent hierarchy. Once you are past that, adding layers helps less than people tend to assume.

So I would put my concern elsewhere. The interesting failures are not that a 100-layer model can't parse a 50-deep bracket sequence. The interesting question is: when the model is uncertain about a nested structure, does it build an approximate, somewhat flat representation that mostly works, the way humans do, and when does that approximation break? And how does the amount of training data control that? That's a learning question, not an expressivity question, and I think that's where the physics-style approach has more to say.

r001.rationale: The response says it is not very concerned in practice: natural language nesting is shallow and decays quickly, so arbitrary-depth limitations matter less than the structures real training data require.

astra-6.text:
I think there is a real limitation in principle, but the question is how much it matters for language in practice. If you construct sentences with more and more levels of nesting, then at some point a transformer of fixed depth may struggle to keep track of that structure. But humans also struggle with deeply nested sentences. We don’t typically communicate that way.

So I would distinguish reproducing the language that people actually use from implementing a rule that works for arbitrarily deep nesting. The second is a much stronger requirement. Failure there would tell us something interesting about the computation the model is doing, but it wouldn’t necessarily mean that it cannot model ordinary language very well.

Where I would be more concerned is when the task really requires a long sequence of dependent reasoning steps. Then the amount of computation available becomes important. And there you have to distinguish a single forward pass from a model that generates intermediate steps, because those give it additional opportunities to compute.

r001.rationale: The response asks how much the limitation matters in practice and distinguishes arbitrary deep nesting from the language people ordinarily use.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a real limitation in principle, but it’s not obvious how important it is in practice. You can construct sentences with arbitrarily deep nesting, and then ask whether a transformer of fixed depth can handle them systematically. That’s a stronger demand than understanding the sentences we normally use. Humans also struggle when you nest clauses too deeply.

So I would distinguish performance on the distribution of natural language from the ability to learn a rule that generalizes to arbitrary depth. A model could be very good at the first and still fail at the second. What would concern me more is if it fails after adding just one or two levels beyond what it saw during training. That would suggest it has learned something less general than the underlying compositional rule.

r001.rationale: The response says the limitation is real in principle but its practical importance is unclear, directly questioning how relevant it is in practice.
